nameStory: The lark bunting gets its name from its lark-like appearance and behavior, especially the male's impressive flight songs that soar high above the prairie like a true lark. Though it's actually a sparrow and not related to larks at all, early settlers noticed how it would rise up from grasslands singing melodiously, just like the skylarks they knew from back home.
description: The lark bunting is a chunky, medium-sized sparrow about the size of a house finch. Males in breeding season are striking with jet-black bodies and bold white wing patches, while females and non-breeding males are brownish with streaky plumage. They have thick, seed-cracking bills and relatively short tails, giving them a compact, robust appearance perfect for life in open grasslands.

idTips.label: Male breeding plumage
idTips.description: Jet-black body with brilliant white wing patches that flash like semaphore flags when the bird flies or displays

idTips.label: Bill shape
idTips.description: Thick, conical seed-cracking bill that looks oversized for the head, pale blue-gray in color

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Undulating flight with alternating flaps and glides, often rising high while singing

idTips.label: Female and winter plumage
idTips.description: Brown and streaky above with lighter underparts, still showing hint of white wing patches

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Stocky and compact with a relatively large head and short tail, giving a chunky silhouette

habitat: In New England, lark buntings are extremely rare vagrants typically found in large, open grasslands, agricultural fields, or airports during migration. They prefer wide-open spaces that mimic their native Great Plains habitat, avoiding forested areas entirely.

seasonality.spring: Rare vagrant during migration, usually May. Males may be developing their striking black breeding plumage.
seasonality.summer: Extremely rare in New England during breeding season. Any sighting would be highly unusual and noteworthy.
seasonality.fall: Most likely time to spot one as a vagrant, August through October. Birds will be in brownish non-breeding plumage.
seasonality.winter: Virtually never seen in New England winters as they migrate to Mexico and the southwestern United States.

funFact: Colorado chose the lark bunting as its state bird in 1931, making it the only state to pick a bird that spends most of the year elsewhere - these nomadic sparrows follow the grass seeds and can completely abandon traditional nesting areas for years if conditions aren't right!
confusionNotes: Female and non-breeding lark buntings can be confused with female bobolinks or large sparrows, but their thick bills, compact shape, and preference for completely open areas help distinguish them. Breeding males are unmistakable with their tuxedo-like black and white pattern.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "bunting," this bird is actually a sparrow in the New World sparrow family. The name reflects historical confusion in bird classification - many chunky, seed-eating birds were labeled "buntings" regardless of their true relationships.
compareHints: Lark buntings are the only species in their genus, making them unique among sparrows. Compared to other New World sparrows, they're much more dependent on wide-open grasslands and show more dramatic seasonal plumage changes. Their closest relatives are probably the towhees and other large, ground-foraging sparrows, but lark buntings are more aerial in their displays and songs.
